primary-verify.summary: Fully verified the two White/Chave/Reynolds(/Van Dover) ALISS vent-light papers by downloading and reading the actual PDFs (JGR 107(B1) doi 10.1029/2000JB000015 via WHOI repository whoi.edu/cms/files/75_121648.pdf; GRL 29(15) doi 10.1029/2002GL014977 via whoi.edu/cms/files/White_02b_46614.pdf). All four targeted figures confirmed with exact quotes and page context, with one important nuance: the estate's figures are real but are per-vent fit values, not universal constants, and Table 1 shows real vent-to-vent spread. The Nakamura/Yamamoto electrochemistry papers themselves (Angew Chem 2010/2013/2017) remain fully paywalled behind Wiley/Cloudflare with no repository or author-page copies found; could not open any of the three primary PDFs directly. However the core ~500 mV redox-gap figure (seawater +478 mV vs SHE, vent fluid -39 mV vs SHE) is strongly triangulated: read in full from the JAMSTEC 2013 Japanese press release (approx 520 mV) and from Yamamoto et al 2022 ISME Journal (open access, read in full: seawater +0.48 V vs SHE, fluid -0.04 V vs SHE, delta 0.52 V, explicitly citing this as measured previously), plus three independent WebSearch snippet syntheses that consistently reproduced the precise 478 mV / -39 mV / 309C / 1053 m / C0014G / Chikyu detail set (almost certainly drawn from Yamamoto et al 2013, the in-situ C0014G electrode paper) - but never got to read that source text directly, so it stays at search-synthesis confidence for the exact two-decimal figures. The 10-210 mV thermoelectric EMF figure surfaced only via WebSearch synthesis (apparently from the Yamamoto/Nakamura/Takai 2018 ChemElectroChem review, itself Cloudflare-blocked) and via mention in a brand-new 2026 Geology paper (also blocked) - unverified by direct reading. Current densities: not located anywhere despite repeated targeted searches; flagged unobtainable this round.

claims.claim: Photon flux of approximately 10^8 photons/cm2/s/sr in the 700-800 nm band (bracketing 750 nm) at the vent orifice. Table 1 of White, Chave & Reynolds 2002 (JGR) gives per-vent values in that band: Lobo 3.3x10^8, Dudley 4.9x10^8, Puffer 7.8x10^7, P Vent 1.6x10^8, Sully 1.6x10^8, L Vent 1.6x10^7 (all photons cm-2 s-1 sr-1). Most vents cluster at approximately 10^8; L Vent is an order lower.
claims.source: White, S.N., Chave, A.D. & Reynolds, G.T., Investigations of ambient light emission at deep-sea hydrothermal vents, J Geophys Res 107(B1), doi 10.1029/2000JB000015, 2002. PDF: https://www.whoi.edu/cms/files/75_121648.pdf, Table 1.

claims.claim: Non-thermal excess light in the 400-600 nm region is on the order of 10^4 photons/cm2/s/sr, versus the 10^2-10^3 photons/cm2/s/sr predicted for pure thermal (blackbody) emission at that wavelength.
claims.source: Same JGR paper, abstract: Temporally variable light is observed in the 400-600 nm region of the spectrum that is orders of magnitude greater than predicted for a thermal source (i.e., on the order of 10^4 rather than 10^2-10^3 photons cm-2 s-1 sr-1). Also repeated in body text for Sully Vent, L Vent, P Vent.

claims.claim: Blackbody fit of 340C with emissivity 0.3 for black-smoker orifice light.
claims.source: Same JGR paper. Exact quotes: The inversion model (photon flux) is plotted as a solid line (340C blackbody of emissivity of 0.3) (P Vent context); The flux at the orifice...corresponds to a 340C blackbody with an emissivity of 0.3 (P Vent); Given a maximum temperature of 340C, an emissivity of 0.3 is required to fit the observed data (Sully Vent). NOTE: this is the fit for specific vents (P Vent, Sully) at their orifice temperature -- other vents in the same paper fit differently: L Vent 295C/0.3, Lobo/Dudley flanges 332C/0.9, Beehive 265C/0.9. It is a representative per-vent fit, not a universal constant.

claims.claim: The primary literature explicitly uses orders of magnitude language (not merely approximately 10x) for the non-thermal 400-600 nm excess, in both ALISS papers.
claims.source: JGR 2002 abstract: observed in the 400-600 nm region of the spectrum that is orders of magnitude greater than predicted for a thermal source. GRL 2002 (White, Chave, Reynolds & Van Dover, Ambient light emission from hydrothermal vents on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, GRL 29(15), doi 10.1029/2002GL014977; PDF https://www.whoi.edu/cms/files/White_02b_46614.pdf): they are known to produce significant light (orders of magnitude above that expected by thermal radiation alone) in the visible region of the spectrum (Introduction).

claims.claim: GRL 2002 (Mid-Atlantic Ridge) paper independently confirms emissivity 0.3 for black smokers and the same order-of-magnitude (10^4 photons/cm2/s/sr) figure for non-thermal short-wavelength excess, at a different ocean basin (Lucky Strike vent, 318C orifice, fit to 300C/0.3 blackbody).
claims.source: Same GRL 2002 PDF: Long wavelength emission...corresponds well to a 300C blackbody with an emissivity of 0.3...The highest quartile shows a peak at 500-550 nm that is on the order of 10^4 photons/cm2/sec/sr.

(2) JAMSTEC official Japanese press release, 2013-09-03 (read in full, PDF https://www.jamstec.go.jp/j/about/press_release/archive/2013/20130903.pdf): states an in-situ measured potential difference of approximately 520 mV between the hydrothermal fluid and surrounding seawater -- also names the artificial vent, 2012 Natsushima/Hyper Dolphin cruise, consistent with Yamamoto 2013 methods. natcomm-2026.summary:
The DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-71131-6 DOES resolve, but it is NOT a primary research paper — it is a Nature Communications 'Comment'/research-briefing piece titled 'From early Earth to Enceladus—mineral electrochemistry could drive organic synthesis' (Nat Commun 17, 3230, 2026; received 11 Feb 2026, accepted 4 Mar, published 9 Apr 2026), sole-authored by Seneca J. Velling (NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory/Caltech; Division of Engineering and Applied Science, Caltech; Kavli Nanoscience Institute, Caltech), who contextualizes and summarizes a companion primary experimental paper published the same day with the adjacent article number: Zhong, Y., Zhang, N., Huan, D. et al. 'Abiotic CO2 reduction promoted by carbonate and phyllosilicate minerals on the primitive seafloor,' Nat Commun 17, 3229 (2026), DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-71130-7 — an 18-author paper led by groups at University of Science and Technology of China (Hefei), with co-authors from ENS de Lyon, Howard University, Tokyo Institute of Technology, Southwest Research Institute (San Antonio), Harvard, and Anhui Normal University.

ACTUAL EXPERIMENTAL WORK (Zhong et al., the primary paper): mineral-coated electrodes of common Ca/Mg carbonates (MCO3) and phyllosilicates, with trace transition-metal cations adsorbed onto the surface (CuCl2/ZnCl2 solutions, at ppm levels comparable to natural oceanic-crust Cu/Zn inventories). Under applied cathodic (negative) potential, adsorbed Cu(II)/Zn(II) were partially reduced to metallic states in/on the mineral, becoming catalytic sites for electrochemical CO2 reduction; the mineral matrix facilitated water dissociation/proton delivery. Zn-doped carbonates favored CO/formate; Cu-doped carbonates extended reduction to CH4 and C2+ products (ethylene, ethanol, acetate); with NH3 present, C-N bond formation occurred, yielding acetamide. Products characterized by 1H NMR and GC/GC-MS-type methods. This is real bench electrochemistry, not a review or pure model. Velling's piece is the accompanying interpretive commentary (with a 'Box 1'/'Box 2' Nernst-equation and CO2-speciation primer) situating the results within measured natural hydrothermal-vent redox potentials (e.g., pH 10 fluid into pH 5.5 seawater at ~250°C shifting E by hundreds of mV; H2 oxidation across pH 2-12, 25-300°C generating potentials from 0 to about -1.1 V vs. SHE) and comparing to Lost City Hydrothermal Field vent-fluid chemistry (elevated formate, acetate, dissolved organic carbon) as a natural benchmark.

EARLY EARTH CLAIM: hydrothermal vent temperature/pH/redox gradients could have supplied the energy for prebiotic CO2-to-organics chemistry on early Earth, with common seafloor carbonates/phyllosilicates (not just previously-emphasized sulfides) as viable catalytic substrates once trace Cu/Zn are adsorbed.

ENCELADUS CLAIM: Enceladus's inferred alkaline, carbonate-bearing ocean and chondritic core (hosting phyllosilicates, sulfides, carbonates), confirmed water-rock interaction, Cassini-detected H2 and complex organics in plume ice grains, and Cassini-detected NH3 together make the mechanism plausible there too — since NH3 is present on Enceladus and the study demonstrated NH3+CO2 -> acetamide, C-N chemistry (peptide-bond-relevant) is suggested as plausible, while explicitly noting this does not distinguish biological from abiotic origin nor prove the mechanism operates there.

SPIN/MAGNETISM/MAGNETITE/CHIRALITY: I searched the complete full text of BOTH the Velling comment and the Zhong et al. primary paper (full HTML article bodies, references, and methods, ~30K and ~65K characters of extracted text respectively) case-insensitively for spin, spintronic, magnet*, chiral*, enantio*, homochiral, and CISS. RESULT: ZERO mentions of spin (in any magnetic/electronic sense), magnetism, magnetite, chirality, enantioselectivity, or CISS in either paper. The only 'magnet-' hits in the primary paper are two incidental mentions of ordinary lab 'magnetic stirring' during mineral preparation, and one mention of 'spinel-group minerals' (a mineral-class name referring to a different prior study's use of a spinel/sulfide mixture as catalyst, not electron spin) — neither is physically related to CISS or homochirality. This is a clean, load-bearing 'no mention at all' finding for the estate's dark-compass hypothesis.

BARGE LINEAGE: The Velling comment explicitly and directly cites Laurie Barge's chemical-garden fuel-cell work twice — Barge, L.M. et al. 'From chemical gardens to fuel cells: generation of electrical potential and current across self-assembling iron mineral membranes,' Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 54, 8184-8187 (2015), cited for 'the same has been shown in the lab scale analogues of hydrothermal chimneys, injection chemical gardens'; and Barge, L.M., Krause, F.C., Jones, J.-P., Billings, K. & Sobron, P. 'Geoelectrodes and fuel cells for simulating hydrothermal vent environments,' Astrobiology 18, 1147-1158 (2018), cited for vents behaving as 'a natural analogue to a fuel cell.' Velling's acknowledgements also thank Dr. Laura M. Barge (NASA JPL/Caltech) and Dr. Jessica M. Weber (NASA JPL/Caltech) by name for 'meaningful suggestions, review of and support in writing this article' — Barge is embedded in this paper's intellectual lineage as advisor/reviewer, not co-author, and her fuel-cell/chemical-garden framework is the explicit conceptual scaffold the whole piece is built on. Both papers frame hydrothermal mineral membranes exactly as Barge's chemical-garden work does: a redox boundary sustaining a measurable electrical potential harvestable for CO2 reduction chemistry — a direct intellectual descendant of that lineage, extending it from sulfides/iron-mineral membranes to carbonates and phyllosilicates.

spring.summary: Research pass on springs and headwaters for the SPRING coining. Springs form by four main geomorphic/hydraulic mechanisms (gravity/descending, artesian/ascending, contact, karst) plus a temperature axis (cold/warm/hot, split at human body temp ~37°C, driven by the ~25-30°C/km geothermal gradient at 1-3 km circulation depth). Their defining ecological property is thermal constancy: Comal Springs (TX) holds ~74°F/23.3°C and San Marcos Springs ~72°F/22.2°C essentially year-round, Silver Springs (FL) sits 68-74°F, and this buffering — because spring water is deep-sourced and shielded from surface weather — makes springs both winter refugia (ice-free) and summer refugia (cool) for aquatic biota. That constancy plus geographic isolation turns spring systems into 'evolutionary archipelagos': Pyrgulopsis springsnails (~120-127 described species, Great Basin alone >80) and stygobiont amphipods (Stygobromus: many single-spring endemics like Stygobromus hayi in DC; Niphargus: >425 species) show narrow single-spring endemism from dispersal on the order of meters to tens of meters/year. Australia's Great Artesian Basin mound springs mirror this exactly: >90 taxa (12 plant, 83 animal) endemic to GAB springs, many 'ultra-short-range endemics' restricted to one spring cluster (e.g., the amphipod Phreatomerus latipes). Groundwater sustains far more of river flow than commonly assumed: global baseflow index ~59%±7% (Jasechko et al. 2024, Nature Geoscience, 15,567 basins); regional figures range from ~48% (Upper Colorado Basin) to ~60-62% (Upper Yellow River, Nida River Poland) to 22-68% (Hawaii streams). The hyporheic zone is the mechanistic link — bidirectional stream/groundwater exchange at cm-to-tens-of-meters scale that acts as a biogeochemical reactor: nitrate removal in hyporheic/engineered systems reaches 68-98%, denitrification dominates once residence time exceeds a threshold (~6.9 h in one study) and can account for ~85% of total nitrate reduction, while the zone also serves as invertebrate refuge/nursery during floods and drought. Snowpack is the seasonal reservoir: in the western US, 53% of total runoff originates as snowmelt despite only 37% of precipitation falling as snow (Li et al. 2017, GRL); in mountainous subregions snowmelt drives 70% of runoff (74% Rockies, 73% Sierra Nevada, 78% Cascades), and a quarter of the West's land area produces 90% of its runoff — feeding ~70 million people. A 2025 USGS study adds a twist: 58%±34% of that snowmelt runoff is itself routed through groundwater before reaching streams, tying the snowpack and baseflow stories together. Karst delivers water fast and dirty by comparison: karst aquifers underlie ~15.2% of ice-free land, host ~1.18 billion people, and supply ~9-10% of the world's drinking water, but their conduit flow means contaminants entering via sinkholes travel with minimal filtration — the tradeoff for karst springs' famously high, concentrated discharge (Florida's Silver Springs: >550 million gallons/day; Idaho's Thousand Springs complex: ~5,200-5,800 cfs average). Finally, headwaters punch far above their weight: estimates of headwater share of total US stream network length range 53-79% depending on methodology, they drain >73% of CONUS land area, and functionally they are the nitrogen-processing bottleneck of river networks — Peterson et al. 2001 (Science) found ammonium is stripped from headwater water within tens to hundreds of meters and nitrate travels only 5-10x that uptake length before removal, while Alexander et al. 2007 (JAWRA) found first-order headwaters contribute ~70% of mean-annual water volume but only ~65% of nitrogen flux reaching second-order streams. Several key primary sources (Peterson 2001, Alexander 2007, Meyer 2007) were paywalled/cookie-walled, so their figures are WebSearch-engine syntheses of abstracts, not directly verified against primary text.

claims.claim: The hyporheic zone is the ecotone of bidirectional stream-groundwater exchange occurring at centimeter-to-tens-of-meters scale (distinguishing it from unidirectional deep groundwater flow); downwelling carries oxygenated surface water and pollutants into sediment, upwelling returns reduced, low-oxygen pore water — this two-way exchange both attenuates pollutants (agricultural, urban, industrial, pathogens) and provides flood/drought refuge and habitat for microorganisms, protists, invertebrates, and fish (an invertebrate nursery function). In engineered/meandering hyporheic systems, nitrate removal reaches 68-98%, with denitrification contributing ~85% of total nitrate reduction (vs. ~10% anammox, ~5% DNRA).

estate_hooks: SPRING (headwaters, this round's target): the discharge-mechanism taxonomy (gravity/artesian/contact/karst/thermal) gives SPRING a clean structure to define against, parallel to how BRINE will define salt's saturation regime and WEDGE defines the estuary ecocline.

Springs-as-refugia (thermal constancy, ±0-2°F year-round at Comal/San Marcos/Silver Springs) structurally echoes the salt-to-fresh circuit's thermal-buffering logic already established for VENT — both are 'constant-condition oases' bracketing the circuit at its two extremes (ultramafic vent heat-buffering vs. spring cold/warm-buffering). Strong candidate for a cross-reference between SPRING and the dark-compass VENT material.

Spring endemism as 'evolutionary archipelago' (Pyrgulopsis, Stygobromus, GAB mound springs, Phreatomerus) is a ready-made counterpoint to SMOLT (the gradient-crosser): SMOLT is defined by traversing gradients, spring endemics by never crossing them — an isolation-vs-dispersal axis that could sharpen both terms by contrast.

Baseflow (59%±7% global, Jasechko 2024) and the snowpack-groundwater linkage (58%±34% of snowmelt routed through groundwater, USGS 2025) suggest SPRING should explicitly claim baseflow as its downstream reach into the river-network circuit — i.e., SPRING is not just the headwater point-source but the sustained fraction of ALL downstream flow, relevant to how the circuit's SEA-to-valley leg gets described.

Karst vulnerability (rapid, low-attenuation conduit transport) is a useful cautionary counterexample to keep 'visible' per the estate's rule: SPRING should not be defined purely as 'pure/protected water source' — karst springs are simultaneously the most abundant (Silver Springs, Thousand Springs discharge figures) and the most contamination-exposed spring type, a built-in tension worth carrying into the coining.

MARSH (salt-marsh REEF-analog, also reserved this round) and the hyporheic zone's biogeochemical-reactor role are structurally parallel — both are ecotones that filter/process material via bidirectional exchange flows rather than one-way transport. Worth flagging for whoever runs the MARSH research pass.

The headwater nitrogen-processing literature (Peterson 2001, Alexander 2007) gives SPRING/headwaters a quantitative 'small but disproportionately powerful' framing (large % of network length/volume, but processes nitrogen at short uptake lengths) that mirrors the axiality conjecture's logic of small local asymmetries producing large systemic effects — a possible thematic bridge worth someone with axiality context evaluating.
surprises: Groundwater's role in mountain snowmelt runoff is counterintuitive: a 2025 study found 58%±34% of western-US snowmelt-derived runoff is itself routed through groundwater before reaching streams — the 'water tower' metaphor undersells how much snowmelt becomes baseflow rather than direct surface runoff.

Karst aquifers are a genuine double-edged case: simultaneously the highest-discharge, most reliable spring type (Silver Springs >550 Mgal/day; Thousand Springs ~5,200-5,800 cfs) and the most contamination-vulnerable groundwater system on Earth, because the same large dissolved conduits that concentrate flow into big springs also transport pollutants with almost no natural filtration.

The percentage of US stream network length classed as 'headwater' varies enormously by methodology — from 53% (EPA) to 79% (recent conterminous-US mapping studies), a >25-point spread that should be flagged rather than smoothed over when the estate cites a single number.

Nitrate travels 5-10x farther than ammonium before being stripped from headwater stream water (Peterson et al. 2001) — a specific, quotable asymmetry in how fast different nitrogen species get processed, more precise than a vague 'headwaters process nitrogen' statement.

Spring endemics show dispersal rates as low as a few meters per year (springsnails), an extraordinarily small number anchoring the 'evolutionary archipelago' framing quantitatively — worth verifying against a primary source before treating as fully load-bearing, since it came through search synthesis rather than a directly read paper.

Several key primary sources (Peterson 2001 Science, Alexander 2007 JAWRA, Meyer 2007 JAWRA) could not be directly read in full — PubMed served only a cookie wall and the JAWRA/Science pages were paywalled — so all figures attributed to them are WebSearch-engine syntheses of abstracts/summaries, not verified against primary text. Flag for primary-source verification before treating as fully load-bearing estate claims.

Research pass on BRINE's cold door — sea-ice brine rejection — covering all six requested threads with sourced, quantitative material. No estate files were written this session (this is a research handoff); the existing notes this builds on are: /home/emsenn/info/lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/science-services-section/services/natural-science-services-section/services/earth-science-services-section/services/hydrology-science-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/2026/08/22/2026-08-22-note-on-the-estuary-and-the-salt-to-fresh-gradient.md (which explicitly flagged brine rejection as untouched, §4) and /home/emsenn/info/lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/science-services-section/services/engineering-science-services-section/services/computer-science-services-section/services/natural-computing-science-services-section/content/text/documents/articles/notes/2026/08/22/2026-08-22-note-on-the-world-of-the-tao-and-the-hydrological-circuit.md (§6, "sea-ice brine rejection ... BRINE's cold door"), plus the BRINE glossary term at /home/emsenn/info/lib/emsenn/services/561-group/services/561-group-services-section/content/text/glossary/terms/bilattice-residuated-ion-normalizing-extremum.md which already names the cold door and cites the mechanism in one sentence pending this research. No existing 561-group section covers oceanography, cryosphere, or astrobiology — the estate's science tree currently runs biological/earth/physical only, so a note built from this research needs a home: either as a companion to the hydrology WEDGE note, or as the founding document of a new oceanography- or cryosphere-science-services-section under earth-science-services-section, matching how hydrology and foraging were founded this session. The Europa material would want either the astronomy-services-section or a new astrobiology section.

PHYSICS. Salt is excluded from the growing ice lattice because ionic solutes cannot substitute into the H2O crystal structure; the rejected solute concentrates as pockets and channels of liquid brine trapped between ice platelets, not diffused ice-bound salt. The brine's salinity at any moment is fixed by thermodynamic equilibrium (the liquidus curve): brine salinity rises steeply as temperature falls, from ~30–35 psu near −1°C to 120–156 psu at −12°C in field observations (White Sea, Jan 2014), approaching saturation near the eutectic. Brine VOLUME fraction (not brine salinity) is the operative variable for ice permeability, given classically by the Frankenstein & Garner (1967) empirical relation Vb = 10⁻³·S·(−49.185/T + 0.532) for −0.5 to −22.9°C (S = bulk ice salinity ppt, T = ice temp °C), later refined by Cox & Weeks (1983). The "law of fives" (properly the Rule of Fives, Golden, Ackley & Lytle, "The Percolation Phase Transition in Sea Ice," Science 282:2238–2241, 1998) is a real percolation-theory result: columnar sea ice is impermeable to fluid flow below a brine volume fraction of ~5%, and permeable above it, because at that threshold isolated brine pockets connect into continuous channels (a genuine physical percolation transition, borrowed from compressed-powder/composite-material math). For typical young ice bulk salinity ~5 ppt, 5% brine volume corresponds to ice temperature ≈ −5°C — hence "fives twice over." Counterexample recorded: granular (frazil) ice, common in Antarctic pancake ice and storm-formed ice, has randomly oriented rather than columnar brine inclusions and shows a measurably HIGHER percolation threshold (~10% brine volume per recent East Antarctic field data) — the Rule of Fives does not transfer to granular ice, a clean prized counterexample. Real phase relationships (Assur 1958 phase diagram, refined by later synchrotron XRD work): as seawater-derived brine cools, minerals precipitate in sequence — ikaite (CaCO3·6H2O) at cold onset (ikaite is thermodynamically stable only below ~7°C generally and precipitates from supersaturated cold brine), mirabilite (Na2SO4·10H2O) at −6.4 to −8.2°C (sources differ: −7.3°C to −8.2°C depending on study), gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) near −15°C, hydrohalite (NaCl·2H2O) at −22.9°C (vs. −21.2°C for pure NaCl solution — seawater's other ions shift it), sylvite (KCl) near −33°C, and finally the eutectic near −36.2°C (seawater) with MgCl2·12H2O, or as low as −53.8°C for the antarcticite (CaCl2·6H2O) pathway under different experimental protocols — genuinely disputed/protocol-dependent eutectics, recorded as live rather than flattened.

DENSE-WATER FORMATION / AABW. Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) is the largest water mass on Earth by volume — 30–40% of total global ocean volume — and forms the abyssal limb of the global overturning circulation. Formation mechanism: brine rejection from sea-ice growth on the continental shelf makes High-Salinity Shelf Water (HSSW) / Dense Shelf Water (DSW), which cascades down the continental slope, entrains ambient Circumpolar Deep Water, and becomes AABW. Global DSW export off Antarctic shelves ≈ 5.4 Sv. In the Atlantic sector (Weddell Sea) specifically, dense water denser than 28.36 kg/m³ exports northward at 8.4 ± 0.7 Sv, composed of 4.5 ± 0.3 Sv well-ventilated DSW plus 3.9 ± 0.5 Sv entrained old Circumpolar Deep Water — meaning even in the best-measured sector, roughly half the exported dense water by this accounting is not fresh brine-rejection product but entrained ambient water; brine rejection is the trigger/densifier, not the sole mass. The Weddell Sea is responsible for up to 50% of total AABW production. Four recognized formation regions: Weddell Sea, Ross Sea, Adélie Coast (Adélie Land/Mertz Glacier polynya), and Cape Darnley (discovered 2013, Ohshima et al., Nature Geoscience). Cape Darnley polynya: wintertime mean DSW export 0.28 Sv; combined with Mackenzie Bay (Prydz Bay region) 1.2 Sv; Cape Darnley Bottom Water is estimated to supply 13–30% of Atlantic-sector AABW production despite being a comparatively narrow shelf with limited storage — demonstrating polynya-driven brine rejection alone, without a large shelf reservoir, can be a major AABW source. Formation is dominated by underwater frazil ice production within polynyas, which (unlike surface congelation ice) has no insulating cover, so ice/brine production per unit area is disproportionately high in a small fraction of total sea-ice area — polynyas are "ice factories."

HABITAT: BRINE CHANNELS, MICROBES, FROST FLOWERS. Brine channels and inclusions host an active microbial community (Sea Ice Microbial Communities, SIMCo) — ice algae (diatoms dominant) and psychrophilic bacteria (chiefly Gammaproteobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, Flavobacteria) that not only survive but actively metabolize and multiply at temperatures down to −20°C and salinities several times seawater's 35 ppt (reported field/lab work places bacteria and algae surviving and functioning in brine at −20°C and correspondingly hypersaline brine, consistent with the liquidus curve which puts brine salinity around 140–160+ ppt near −10 to −12°C, rising further toward −20°C). This SIMCo forms a discrete microbial loop supporting metazoan grazers and is a major food source underpinning polar trophic webs (ice algae blooms feed Antarctic krill directly). Distinct hypersaline cryopeg brine communities (subzero, permanently liquid brine pockets in permafrost/coastal sea ice) show taxonomically distinct assemblages from the overlying sea ice proper. Frost flowers: ice crystals that condense on the brine-wetted surface of new, thin sea ice (nilas), fed by capillary wicking of a highly saline "brine skim" (salinity ~100–200 psu) that forms on the surface during rapid freezing; frost flower salinity itself runs 77–125 psu, roughly 10× the 6–11 psu salinity of the young ice surface beneath them, with brine contributing 50–80% of frost-flower mass by capillary wicking. Frost flowers and the brine skim are a recognized major source of sea-salt aerosol and halogen (bromine) chemistry over sea ice, linking brine rejection directly to polar atmospheric chemistry (ozone depletion events).

MINERAL PRECIPITATION: IKAITE. Ikaite (CaCO3·6H2O) is the calcium-carbonate hexahydrate that precipitates specifically in cold, high-alkalinity brine — it is NOT stable at room temperature (decomposes rapidly above ~7°C, which is why it is essentially unknown outside cold/deep-sea/sea-ice settings) and requires the elevated pH and supersaturation that concentrating sea-ice brine produces. Documented in both Arctic (north of Svalbard) and Antarctic sea ice. Its precipitation releases CO2 (removing carbonate ions to solid CaCO3 releases dissolved CO2 to solution/atmosphere), while the associated dense, cold, CO2-loaded brine sinks with the AABW/DSW brine-rejection plume — proposed as a "sea-ice-driven carbon pump" component of the polar carbon cycle, actively researched, not settled.

DESALINATION TRAJECTORY (multi-year ice). Newly frozen seawater brine-rejects hard: first-year sea ice bulk salinity starts >10 ppt (initial freezing) and falls to <5 ppt within the first winter via gravity drainage (brine channels draining under gravity) and brine expulsion. Through the first summer, surface and internal meltwater "flushing" is the single most effective desalination step — meltwater percolating downward physically displaces residual brine, faster than winter gravity drainage alone. By the time ice has survived multiple melt seasons (true multi-year ice), average bulk salinity has dropped to 3–4 ppt, with the surface layer essentially fully desalinated; some sources report multi-year ice or its melt-pond water below 1–2 ppt. Multi-year ice at this salinity is reported (search-synthesis level sourcing, matches multiple independent tertiary sources, not yet a primary paper directly read) as genuinely usable as drinking water and historically used this way by Inuit hunters and polar sailors, especially melt-pond water pooling on its surface, which runs fresher than the ice's own bulk salinity. Caveat for the eventual note: WHO/typical potability guidelines sit near 1 ppt (1000 mg/L TDS); 3–4 ppt bulk multi-year ice is on the edge of palatable/potable and the strongest "drinkable" claims in the tertiary literature likely refer preferentially to melt-pond water rather than bulk ice melt — flag as needing a primary-source check before being stated as settled science.

OCEAN-WORLD ANALOGS. Europa's "chaos terrain" — geologically young, chaotically disrupted ice-shell surface — is now the leading hypothesis-space for shallow (roughly 1–5 km depth) liquid brine reservoirs ("cryomagma") within the ice shell itself, distinct from the deep global ocean beneath. As these shallow brine pockets freeze, they pressurize (freezing brine expands / concentrates residual liquid, raising pressure), a proposed trigger mechanism for cryovolcanic eruption of brine onto the surface — directly the Europan analog of terrestrial brine rejection's physics (freezing concentrates and pressurizes residual liquid) applied to an ice shell instead of sea ice. This is active, current (2024–2025) research explicitly framed around future mission observations (implicitly Europa Clipper) rather than settled fact — recorded as a live research frontier, not confirmed detection.

surprises: The Rule of Fives is not universal: granular/frazil Antarctic sea ice has a distinctly higher percolation threshold (~10% brine volume) than the classic columnar-ice 5% figure, meaning the famous 'law of fives' is columnar-ice-specific, not a general sea-ice constant — this is exactly the kind of counterexample the estate's rule prizes and would be easy to accidentally over-generalize.

Brine rejection is only part of the AABW story even in its best-studied sector: in the Atlantic sector's 8.4 Sv dense-water export, nearly half (3.9 of 8.4 Sv) is entrained ambient Circumpolar Deep Water rather than freshly brine-rejected shelf water — brine rejection densifies and triggers the cascade but isn't the majority of the exported mass by this accounting, a nuance easy to flatten into 'AABW = brine rejection.'

tidal-pumping.summary: Researched the moon's half of the WEDGE — tidal pumping and the estuary — across seven required sub-topics: the mixing-mechanism classification literature (horizontal/Simpson Richardson number, Simpson's strain-induced periodic stratification), the tidal prism and flushing time, tidal freshwater zones, tidal asymmetry and sediment pumping, estuarine turbidity maximum (ETM) dynamics, spring-neap modulation of stratification and hypoxia, and tidal bores as the extreme case. No estate file was written — this is a research-gathering pass; the parallel session is already actively rewriting `2026-08-22-note-on-the-estuary-and-the-salt-to-fresh-gradient.md` and the WEDGE glossary term, both of which explicitly flag tidal pumping as the missing piece this report supplies. All findings below are sourced by URL with an access-confidence tag; two items are flagged as corrections against commonly-repeated figures (Qiantang bore speed/height, and the internal disagreement between two published Simpson-number critical values), consistent with the estate's rule to carry disputes visibly rather than flatten them.

claims.claim: The Simpson (horizontal Richardson) number Si characterizes the balance of stratifying buoyancy input against destratifying tidal-stirring energy in an estuary; Si ~ 0.1 marks the transition between well-mixed and periodically stratified conditions, built from the potential energy anomaly (φ) framework of Simpson (1981).
claims.source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1447316/full and related search synthesis on the Simpson number

claims.claim: Two published critical Si thresholds disagree and are recorded as a live discrepancy rather than flattened: Stacey & Ralston (2005) give Si ≈ 0.2 as the ebb-tide transition to full mixing, while other cited work gives Si ≈ 0.84 as the flood-tide critical value, with an intermediate periodic-stratification regime reported as 0.088 < Si < 0.84 across mean-to-spring tides.
claims.source: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/marine-science/articles/10.3389/fmars.2025.1447316/full

claims.claim: Simpson, J.H., Brown, J., Matthews, J., Allen, G. (1990), "Tidal Straining, Density Currents, and Stirring in the Control of Estuarine Stratification," Estuaries 13(2):125-132, DOI 10.2307/1351581, is the founding paper defining strain-induced periodic stratification (SIPS): the vertically sheared flood/ebb current acting on a longitudinal salinity gradient alternately stratifies (flood) and destratifies (ebb) the water column within a single tidal cycle, faster than the tidal period itself.
claims.source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.2307/1351581 (citation confirmed via ResearchGate/Springer listings); full text unreachable, ResearchGate PDF returned HTTP 403

claims.claim: SIPS has been directly observed and remains an active research target, e.g. in the Guadalquivir and Weser estuaries, where modern modeling papers (Copernicus Ocean Science 2022 on the Weser) build on the Simpson framework.
claims.source: https://os.copernicus.org/articles/18/1725/2022/ ; ResearchGate SIPS-Guadalquivir listing

claims.claim: A formula circulating for an "estuarine/Richardson-estuary number" attributed to Fischer (1972) is Ri_E ∝ g(Δρ/ρ)·Q_R·T³ / (ρ·b·L³), combining freshwater discharge Q_R, tidal period T, mouth width b and tidal excursion L — this specific rendering could not be checked against Fischer's original 1972 J. Fluid Mech. paper ("Mass transport mechanisms in partially stratified estuaries," 53:671-687) and its dimensional consistency is not confirmed; flagged as unverified pending primary-source access, and should not be inserted into a note as a citable equation without that check.
claims.source: https://www.coastalwiki.org/wiki/Seawater_intrusion_and_mixing_in_estuaries

claims.claim: Tidal prism is the volume of water exchanged through an estuary/inlet mouth between mean low and mean high water (excluding river discharge), approximated as P = H x A (tidal range times basin surface area); larger tidal prisms correlate with larger ebb-tidal-delta sand deposits (Walton & Adams relationship).
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_prism

claims.claim: Worked example, Okatee River estuary (South Carolina): tidal prism P = 7.11 x 10^5 m3, estuary volume V ~ 5.9 x 10^5 m3, giving a tidal-prism-method flushing time of Tf ~ 2.3 days — a lower-bound estimate, valid chiefly for well-mixed to slightly stratified estuaries.
claims.source: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2005JC003041 (Moore 2006, J. Geophys. Res. Oceans)

claims.claim: Real-estuary tidal prism magnitudes are on the order of 10^9 m3: San Francisco Bay ~ 1.59 x 10^9 m3 (~1.3 million acre-feet); Chesapeake Bay, M2-constituent tidal prism ~ 1.25 x 10^9 m3 — comparable orders of magnitude despite very different geometries.
claims.source: search synthesis referencing Grokipedia/USGS San Francisco Bay bathymetry and Chesapeake Bay Tidal Characteristics (SCIRP/ResearchGate)

claims.claim: A tidal freshwater zone (TFZ) is a transitional river reach with freshwater chemistry (no measurable salt) but full tidal physics — bidirectional currents and water-level oscillation — bounded formally by three longitudinal markers: the upstream limit of brackish water, the upstream limit of bidirectional tidal velocity, and the upstream limit of tidal-stage fluctuation (Jones et al. 2020, Water Resources Research, DOI 10.1029/2019WR026619). Its length is dynamic, contracting under low baseflow (salt encroaches upstream) and elongating rapidly during high-runoff events.
claims.source: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2019WR026619 (full text blocked, HTTP 403; relied on search-engine synthesis of the abstract)

claims.claim: Tidal influence and tidal freshwater zones commonly extend 10-100+ km upstream of the coast: the Hudson River estuary is tidal for roughly 120+ km of its 153-mile (246 km) length; the Delaware Estuary shows near-constant tidal amplitude for its downstream ~150 km (friction and channel convergence balance); the Potomac and Incomati rivers are cited as comparable examples.
claims.source: search synthesis of Hudson River NERR (coast.noaa.gov), NJ DRBC river-mileage data, and general tidal-river literature

claims.claim: Tidal asymmetry — flood-dominant (shorter, higher-velocity flood; longer, lower-velocity ebb) versus ebb-dominant tides — arises from nonlinear (shallow-water) distortion of the tidal wave as it propagates into a shoaling, converging estuary, and is the mechanism, distinct from river discharge, that determines whether an estuary imports (flood-dominant -> infills/shoals) or exports (ebb-dominant) sediment net of a tidal cycle.
claims.source: https://geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Oceanography/Coastal_Dynamics_(Bosboom_and_Stive)/05:_Coastal_hydrodynamics/5.07:_Tidal_propagation_in_coastal_waters/5.7.4:_Tidal_asymmetry ; https://www.coastalwiki.org/wiki/Morphology_of_estuaries

claims.claim: Because sediment resuspension scales strongly with flow velocity, flood-dominant asymmetry makes the suspended load carried landward on flood far exceed the load carried seaward on the weaker ebb — this net landward pumping of sediment is itself called "tidal pumping" in the sediment-transport literature, and is the standard explanation for why many macrotidal estuaries progressively infill/shoal.
claims.source: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/2014JC010228 (Yu et al. 2014, JGR Oceans, "Turbidity maximum formation in a well-mixed macrotidal estuary: the role of tidal pumping")

claims.claim: The estuarine turbidity maximum (ETM) is a convergence zone of suspended sediment located near the landward limit of salinity intrusion, sustained by a combination of gravitational (density-driven) circulation, tidal pumping/straining, resuspension-settling cycling, and topographic trapping — foundational mechanistic accounts trace to Postma (1967) and later Geyer-lineage work.
claims.source: https://www.coastalwiki.org/wiki/Estuarine_turbidity_maximum ; https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-marine-010816-060535

claims.claim: ETM suspended-sediment concentrations are dramatically elevated versus background: open river/coastal water is typically <10-100 mg/L, the ETM proper reaches several g/L averaged over the water column, and where concentrations exceed roughly 1,000 g/L (~1 kg/L) the material behaves as fluid mud; the Loire and Gironde estuaries (France) are named examples of persistently high-turbidity systems, with the Gironde noted as an especially efficient sediment trap.
claims.source: https://www.coastalwiki.org/wiki/Estuarine_turbidity_maximum

claims.claim: The ETM is under direct tidal (spring-neap) control: during neap tides, longer slack-water periods let sediment settle and consolidate into fluid mud; spring tides resuspend that accumulated mud, producing peak turbidity. In the Oujiang Estuary (China), the ETM's position migrates with the fortnightly cycle — sitting near Qingshuipu (upstream) under spring-tide landward tidal-pumping transport, and relocating downstream to Zhenhai under neap-tide gravitational circulation, with lateral (north/south) shifts also tracking spring/neap mixing strength.
claims.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278434323000018 (Oujiang Estuary case study)

claims.claim: Spring-neap tidal cycling modulates estuarine mixing and stratification on fortnightly and monthly timescales: 3D hydrodynamic modeling of Chesapeake Bay shows turbulent mixing and vertical stratification undergoing large fortnightly (spring-neap) as well as tidal (flood-ebb) fluctuations.
claims.source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0278434307001859 (Flood-Ebb and Spring-Neap Variations of Mixing, Stratification and Circulation in Chesapeake Bay)

claims.claim: In Chesapeake Bay, hypoxic (bottom dissolved-oxygen-depleted) areal extent has been shown to shrink through the neap-to-spring tidal transition: reduced stratification and stronger currents during spring tide promote mixing/reaeration that erodes the hypoxic pool, while stratification (and hypoxia) rebuild toward neap tide — layered on top of the larger seasonal hypoxia cycle that begins in the upper mesohaline in late spring and expands down-estuary by early summer.
claims.source: search synthesis of Chesapeake Bay hypoxia modeling literature (darchive.mblwhoilibrary.org; Springer "Physical controls on hypoxia" chapter)

claims.claim: General stratification-hypoxia relationship: stratification impedes vertical exchange of dissolved oxygen between surface and bottom waters, while tidal stirring promotes turbulence and reaeration; hypoxia risk is therefore highest where stratification is strong relative to tidal mixing, a pattern reported for both micro-tidal (e.g. Chesapeake Bay) and some meso-tidal systems.
claims.source: search synthesis (general estuarine hypoxia literature, cross-referenced against Chesapeake- and Yangtze-estuary hypoxia papers)

claims.claim: A tidal bore forms where a large tidal range (commonly cited threshold ~6 m, some sources say 6-9 m) is funneled by a shoaling, converging, shallow river mouth into a single upstream-propagating surge; the surge's structure is set by its Froude number — undular (smooth wave-train) bores below roughly Fr 1.2-1.3, breaking bores above that, fully broken/turbulent bores above Fr ~ 1.7.
claims.source: https://staff.civil.uq.edu.au/h.chanson/tid_bore.html (Hubert Chanson, University of Queensland, leading academic authority on tidal bore hydrodynamics) and https://doi.org/10.3390/su17167363

claims.claim: Qiantang River bore (Hangzhou Bay, China), the world's most powerful bore, in an academically-sourced quantitative profile: the lower 85 km reach (below Ganpu) has an annual mean tidal range of 5.62 m and a maximum of 9 m at Ganpu; bore height is typically 1-3 m during spring tide, with 4 m a common maximum and 9 m recorded only as an extreme outlier; the bore travels more than 100 km upstream at 20-30 km/h during spring tide.
claims.source: https://doi.org/10.3390/su17167363 ("Hydrodynamics of the Qiantang Tidal Bore and Its Responses to Embankment, Morphology, and River Discharge") and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1001605811603870 (experimental hydrodynamic study)

claims.claim: CORRECTION flagged: popular/tourism-oriented sources commonly repeat a Qiantang bore top speed of ~40 km/h and imply 9 m as a typical rather than extreme height; the peer-reviewed hydrodynamics literature instead gives 20-30 km/h propagation speed and 1-3 m as the typical spring-tide bore height, with 9 m recorded only as an outlier maximum. The estate should carry the academic figures as primary and flag the popular figures as inflated, per the estate's rule to prefer sourced, quantitative claims.
claims.source: Comparison of https://doi.org/10.3390/su17167363 (academic) against general web search synthesis of tourism/amusement sites for the 40 km/h and "up to 9 m typical" framing

claims.claim: Severn Bore (England, River Severn): height up to roughly 2-2.7 m on exceptional tides, travels close to 20 miles (~32 km) upstream, ridden by surfers for over an hour in favorable conditions — among the world's most consistently surfed bores.
claims.source: https://www.rapturecamps.com/blog/tidal-bore-surfing-explained ; https://surfholidays.com/blog/surfing-tidal-bores-the-worlds-top-7/

claims.claim: Pororoca (Amazon River system, Brazil): bore waves up to 4 m high, traveling as much as 800 km inland upstream on the Amazon and adjacent rivers, advancing at 16-24 km/h (10-15 mph).
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pororoca

claims.claim: Petitcodiac River bore (Bay of Fundy system, Canada) formerly exceeded 2 m in height before a mid-20th-century causeway suppressed it; restoration efforts beginning around 2010 (partial causeway removal) have worked to revive the bore, illustrating that tidal bores are anthropogenically alterable/destroyable, not fixed natural constants.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_bore

claims.claim: A smaller, precisely instrumented bore case (Sélune River, Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel, France) gives fine-grained quantitative bore mechanics: on a 13.75 m tidal-range day, bore front celerity was measured at 2.7-3.1 m/s entering the river mouth, slowing to 2.5-2.7 m/s further upstream, with a modest bore height of only 0.3-0.6 m — showing that even the world's largest tidal-range region (Bay of Fundy/Mont-Saint-Michel) does not guarantee a large bore; channel convergence/shallowness geometry matters as much as tidal range.
claims.source: https://staff.civil.uq.edu.au/h.chanson/tid_bore.html

claims.claim: The Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's largest tidal range, and its Salmon River (Truro, Nova Scotia) hosts a notable bore within that system, tying the extreme-tidal-range end of the phenomenon to a specific, named, documented location.
claims.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_bore

claims.claim: Circatidal (~12.4 h) biological clocks exist as molecularly distinct oscillators from circadian (~24 h) clocks: in the intertidal isopod Eurydice pulchra, knockdown of core circadian genes (period, bmal1, clock) disrupts circadian but not circatidal locomotor rhythms (though bmal1 is needed to coordinate circatidal timing across behaviors), and peroxiredoxin redox-oscillation rhythms suggest circatidal timing may ride a separate, non-transcriptional metabolic oscillator — direct evidence that the moon's forcing writes its own biological clock, independent of the sun's.
claims.source: 561-group estate record, scout-1-planetary-tier-report.md, line 23, citing Zhang et al./Wilcockson & Zhang lab, PLOS Genetics 2023; O'Neill et al., Curr. Biol. 2013/2015

estate_hooks: Directly answers the gap explicitly flagged in both the existing estuary note (Section 1 scope note: 'this treatment is river-discharge-centric... the dominant mixing mechanism is tidal pumping... a full treatment needs both') and the WEDGE glossary term's Exchanging etymology ('tidal exchange... twice a day the moon drives the mixing that river discharge alone would not accomplish') — this report is the material that etymology gestures at but the note doesn't yet cite.

SPRING (headwaters, this round's reserved seat): the tidal freshwater zone is precisely the reach between SPRING's fresh, non-tidal headwaters and the salt front — tidal but fresh, the physical bridge between the two reserved-seat niches (SPRING and WEDGE) that the estate has been treating as separate.

MARSH (salt-marsh REEF-analog, this round's reserved seat): flood-dominant tidal asymmetry and tidal pumping are literally the accretion mechanism that builds and maintains salt marsh platforms — the same landward sediment-import process that fills/shoals estuary channels also supplies the sediment MARSH would need for its REEF-analog framing (reef accretion vs. marsh accretion as parallel gradient-fed structures).

BRINE (this round's target, sea-ice brine rejection): not directly connected by the mechanisms researched here, but spring-neap salinity/stratification cycling in estuaries is a second, distinct 'salt regime that varies on a lunar clock' — worth a cross-reference note that BRINE's cold-door mechanism and the WEDGE's tidal mechanism are both moon-modulated salt stories, on different clocks (freeze-thaw vs. fortnightly).

The circatidal-clock material (Eurydice pulchra, already in scout-1-planetary-tier-report.md but unused in any note) belongs squarely under this mission's 'moon's half of the WEDGE' framing — it is the biological-clock evidence that the tide is not just a hydrodynamic forcing but an entrained physiological one, a natural-computing angle the estate's SMOLT/WEDGE material hasn't yet reached.

The Qiantang bore correction (academic 20-30 km/h and 1-3 m typical vs. popular-source 40 km/h and 9 m typical) is a ready-made instance of the estate's own 'corrections and disputes carried visibly' rule — structurally identical to the Murchison/Ozturk/parity-violation corrections already logged in scout-2-homochirality-verification-report.md.

ETM flocculation-and-trapping material extends (does not contradict) the existing note's flocculation section: the note already has 'why mud flocculates'; this report supplies 'why it re-concentrates and stays put at a specific, tidally-migrating location' — the missing back half of the MUD-formation story.

The Fischer (1972) Richardson-number formula could not be verified against the primary paper and should NOT be inserted into any note as a citable equation without a primary-source read; flagged explicitly so a synthesis pass doesn't silently promote an unverified formula to load-bearing status.
surprises: The Qiantang bore's headline stats are less extreme in the peer-reviewed literature than in popular retellings: typical spring-tide bore height is 1-3 m (not the commonly quoted 9 m, which is an extreme outlier), and propagation speed is academically given as 20-30 km/h, not the 40 km/h figure that circulates on tourism sites.

Tidal range alone does not predict bore size: the Sélune River case (Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel) had a 13.75 m tidal range — genuinely enormous — yet produced only a 0.3-0.6 m bore, because channel convergence/shallowness geometry matters as much as tidal-range magnitude. This complicates any simple 'bigger tide = bigger bore' framing.

Published critical values for the Simpson number itself disagree by roughly 4x depending on tidal phase and source (Si ~ 0.2 on ebb per Stacey & Ralston 2005 vs. Si ~ 0.84 on flood per other cited work) — the estate's rule to carry disputes visibly applies to a core dimensionless number in the mixing-classification literature, not just to headline biology/geology claims.

Tidal bores are not fixed natural constants: the Petitcodiac River bore was largely destroyed by a mid-20th-century causeway and is only now being partially restored — the 'extreme case' of tidal mixing is itself infrastructure-vulnerable.

Spring-neap modulation of ETM position can be a real spatial migration, not just an intensity change: in the Oujiang Estuary the turbidity maximum's location itself shifts (Qingshuipu on spring tide vs. Zhenhai on neap), driven by a switch between tidal-pumping-dominated and gravitational-circulation-dominated transport regimes.

The Fischer (1972) Richardson-number formula for estuaries proved surprisingly hard to pin down from secondary sources — the version found (via Coastal Wiki) has a suspicious dimensional structure (rho appears to cancel incompletely) and should be treated as unverified rather than inserted as a citable equation.

marsh-peat.summary: Compiled a quantitative, sourced literature base for MARSH (salt-marsh accretion/peat, the estuary's REEF-analog). All access was via WebSearch synopses of search results — every primary-source WebFetch attempt in this session was blocked (403/405/login-redirect on ScienceDirect, Science, AdsAbs, Nature), so nothing below was read in full text; treat quantitative figures as needing a primary-source read-through before they're load-bearing in the estate record. Coverage: (1) Vertical accretion rates run from ~0.9-17.8 mm/yr in short-term marker-horizon/SET studies (e.g. Texas: 1.9-11.9 mm/yr) down to 0.6-5 mm/yr in millennial radiocarbon-dated basal-peat records (Great Sippewissett avg 3.13 mm/yr) - short-term and long-term (compaction-integrated) accretion rates are genuinely different quantities and get conflated in casual citation. (2) Mineral vs. organic contribution is site-dependent, not universal: North Sea marshes accrete mainly via allochthonous mineral sedimentation, New England marshes (Great Sippewissett) mainly via root/rhizome burial; one synthesis found organic accumulation explaining 59% of accretion variance and outweighing inorganic 5:1, while another flagged organic matter's accretion contribution declining ~22% recently, linked to warming-driven decomposition - a live tension worth carrying, not resolving. (3) Spartina/Salicornia are demonstrated ecosystem engineers: stem density slows flow and raises mineral deposition within vegetated patches, roots bind sediment, and Spartina anglica tussocks trigger a local positive feedback (elevation gain -> tussock expansion -> marsh succession) - the biogeomorphic engine of MARSH-as-REEF-analog. (4) Marsh peat is real but young relative to coral reefs: basal peat dates cluster in the Mid-Holocene, commonly 3,000-6,000 cal yr BP (Great Bay NH basal date ~4,560 cal yr BP; a Plum Island-region marsh initiated ~3.3 ka); NE US marshes as a class only initiated once early-Holocene sea-level rise slowed below ~6,000 yr BP - the REEF analogy holds mechanistically (generations building on predecessors' root mats) but not in absolute antiquity; reef sequences run far older. (5) Keeping pace with SLR has hard, numbered thresholds: marsh drowning within centuries above ~3 mm/yr relative SLR, conversion to open water within ~50 years above 6-9 mm/yr; a marsh/mangrove adjustment deficit is 'likely' at 4 mm/yr RSLR and 'highly likely' at 7 mm/yr (Saintilan et al., Science 2022). Loss is not just submergence: pond formation inside marsh interiors produces power-law, self-similar pond-size distributions and a 'doughnut-like' fragmentation pattern (edges keep accreting via allochthonous sediment access, interiors starve and drown) - directly matches the 'runaway ecocline' framing. (6) Blue carbon: salt-marsh soil carbon burial averages ~218-245 g C/m2/yr (Ouyang & Lee 2014: 244.7+/-26.1, with real regional spread e.g. N. Europe 315.2+/-62.9; range across sites 19-1,713 g C/m2/yr) against terrestrial forest soil accumulation of roughly 4-13 g C/m2/yr depending on synthesis - order-of-magnitude 'burial rate 10-50x forest' claims are real but the exact multiplier is synthesis-dependent. Global soil stock ~1.4-2.4 Pg C in the top ~1 m of the world's tidal marshes (two independent recent estimates converge); despite marshes' tiny footprint their total annual burial (5-87 Tg C/yr, wide uncertainty) is roughly comparable to whole-biome-total forest soil burial (49-79 Tg C/yr per biome). Global marsh area itself is contested: a 2020 remote-sensing estimate gives 52,880 km2, but older literature spans 22,000-400,000 km2 (20-fold uncertainty). Marshes are also currently shrinking: net loss of 719 km2 (2000-2019, ~0.28%/yr), 16.3 Tg CO2e/yr net emissions from that loss. (7) Dieback and recovery are real, multi-causal, and partly reversible: 'sudden vegetation dieback' hit Atlantic/Gulf marshes 2000-2002, driven by drought-stressed Spartina made vulnerable to periwinkle snail (Littoraria irrorata) grazing fronts; when snails were experimentally excluded, cordgrass resprouted - direct causal demonstration. estate_hooks: MARSH-as-REEF-analog holds mechanistically (vegetation-trapped sediment + buried root mat = generations building on ancestors' remains, exactly parallel to coral) but breaks on absolute antiquity: marsh peat sequences bottom out at Mid-Holocene basal dates (~3,000-6,000 cal yr BP) because early-Holocene sea-level rise outran accretion everywhere until it slowed - worth stating explicitly as where the REEF analogy is structural, not temporal.

The accretion-deficit thresholds (3 mm/yr drowning-within-centuries; 6-9 mm/yr conversion-within-50-years; 'likely deficit' at 4 mm/yr, 'highly likely' at 7 mm/yr) give BRINE's sea-level-rise context a numeric backbone if the estate wants to connect marsh fate to the salt-to-fresh water circuit's downstream (estuary/WEDGE) segment.

The 'doughnut-like fragmentation' / runaway pond-drowning dynamic is the clearest literal match to 'runaway ecocline dynamics' named in the mission brief - a good candidate mechanism to formalize under whatever the estate's ecocline-dynamics vocabulary ends up being, alongside WEDGE.

The outwelling hypothesis's three-act history (Odum proposed -> Nixon debunked -> blue-carbon era revived via a different mechanism) is a strong worked example for the estate's 'corrections and disputes carried visibly' rule - it is not merely a fact but a case study in how the field itself corrected and re-corrected.

The IPCC-vs-Ouyang&Lee threefold disagreement on global marsh CAR (91 vs 245 g C/m2/yr) and the 20-fold uncertainty in global marsh area (22,000-400,000 km2) are two more concrete disputes to carry visibly rather than resolve prematurely.

SMOLT (the gradient-crosser) and MARSH (the standing accretor) sit at opposite ends of a mobility spectrum within the same estuary system - one traverses the salinity gradient, the other builds vertically against sea-level rise; both are literally contending with the same physical gradient (salt intrusion, tidal flux) via opposite strategies (motion vs. accretion), which may be worth a cross-reference note when MARSH is formally coined.
surprises: Short-term (marker-horizon) and long-term (radiocarbon-dated peat) marsh accretion rates are genuinely different quantities that get casually conflated in the literature - short-term rates run several mm/yr to >1 cm/yr, long-term rates run sub-mm to a few mm/yr, likely because peat compaction and burial diagenesis integrate the record differently than a fresh marker horizon.

Organic matter's contribution to marsh accretion appears to be declining in recent decades (~22% average decline cited), plausibly a direct signature of warming-driven decomposition eating into the marsh's own carbon-burial engine - a feedback that could matter for the estate's broader carbon/climate threads.

Salt marshes are NOT ancient the way reefs are: nearly every dated marsh peat sequence in the literature bottoms out in the Mid-Holocene (last ~6,000 years), because marshes literally could not exist as continuous structures earlier - the sea was rising too fast for any vegetation-accretion feedback to establish. The REEF-analog is doing real conceptual work but should not imply comparable timescales.

The outwelling hypothesis is a genuine two-reversal story, not a single settled fact: real science (1968) -> real refutation (1980) -> real partial revival via a different causal mechanism (2020s) - all three stages are independently well-documented, making it an unusually clean case study of self-correcting science for the estate's methodology.
